section_title: Historical problems in the Old Testament
title: Solomon's Temple: a huge workforce for a small building

rows.thesis: 1 Kings says Solomon used more than 180,000 workers for seven years to build a temple roughly 27 metres long and 9 metres wide, about the floor area of a large house. The numbers are not credible as history.
rows.arg:
P1 A historical record should give numbers that fit the work described. 
 P2 The Bible gives a labour force of over 180,000 men for seven years (1 Kgs 5:13-16; 6:38) to build a stone building of 60 by 20 cubits (1 Kgs 6:2), while archaeologists estimate the whole population of Judah in the 10th century BCE at only a few tens of thousands. 
 ∴ The figures are exaggerated, which shows the account is not an exact historical record.
rows.ev:
The workforce. "King Solomon drafted forced labour out of all Israel, and the draft numbered 30,000 men… Solomon also had 70,000 burden-bearers and 80,000 stonecutters in the hill country, besides 3,300 chief officers" (1 Kgs 5:13-16). That is 183,300 men. 2 Chronicles 2:18 gives 3,600 officers instead of 3,300.

 The time. "He was seven years in building it" (1 Kgs 6:38). His own palace took thirteen (7:1).

 The building. "The house that King Solomon built for the LORD was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high" (1 Kgs 6:2): about 27 by 9 metres, roughly 240 square metres of floor, plus a porch and side rooms.

 The population. Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman ( The Bible Unearthed , 2001) estimate the population of the Judean highlands in the 10th century BCE at around 5,000 people in some twenty small villages, and Jerusalem as no more than a modest town. Even the higher estimates of other archaeologists cannot supply 183,000 labourers.

 The gold. David is said to have set aside 100,000 talents of gold and a million talents of silver for the Temple (1 Chr 22:14). A talent was roughly 30-34 kg, so that is over 3,000 tonnes of gold, comparable to the whole world's annual gold mining today, for a small hill kingdom.
rows.obj:
"The workers built Solomon's palace and other projects too."
 The text ties the levy specifically to the Temple (1 Kgs 5:5, 17-18). And even spread across all his building, 183,000 workers exceeds the population archaeology allows for the region.


 "Archaeologists like Eilat Mazar found Solomonic structures."
 Mazar's identifications are disputed, and even if accepted they show a modest administrative centre, not an empire able to field nearly 200,000 labourers and thousands of tonnes of gold.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “You're relying on Finkelstein, a minimalist.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer Finkelstein is a mainstream Israeli archaeologist, not a minimalist. But set his population estimate aside: 3,000 tonnes of gold for a temple in a hill kingdom is impossible on any reckoning, and Kings and Chronicles don't even agree on the number of officers.
rows.sum: 183,300 workers for seven years and over 3,000 tonnes of gold for a building of about 27 by 9 metres, in a region whose population archaeologists put in the thousands or low tens of thousands. The figures are not history.

section_title: Historical problems in the Old Testament
title: The Exodus and the wilderness leave no trace

rows.thesis: The Bible describes over two million Israelites leaving Egypt and living forty years in Sinai. Egyptian records never mention it and excavations at the key wilderness sites have found nothing from that period. The Quran, by contrast, never gives the inflated numbers.
rows.arg:
P1 An event on the scale described would leave archaeological or documentary traces. 
 P2 Two million people over forty years would leave camps, graves and pottery, and the loss of the slave workforce and Pharaoh's army would appear somewhere in Egyptian records. None of this has been found; Kadesh-barnea, where Israel stayed 38 years, has no remains from the right period. 
 ∴ The biblical account, at least in its numbers, is not historical; the Quran's account (a "small band", 26:54) avoids the problem.
rows.ev:
The numbers. 600,000 men on foot besides women and children (Exod 12:37); the census in Numbers 1:46 gives exactly 603,550 fighting men. With families that is two to three million people, more than the estimated population of Egypt at the time.

 No Egyptian record. Egyptian sources mention Semitic workers and the Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BCE) mentions "Israel" as a people in Canaan, but no Egyptian text mentions a mass departure, plagues or the loss of an army.

 The wilderness. Excavations at Kadesh-barnea (Tell el-Qudeirat) by Rudolph Cohen found no remains earlier than the 10th century BCE. Finkelstein and Silberman write that repeated surveys of Sinai have found no evidence of the wanderings.

 Contrast with the Quran. The Quran's Pharaoh calls the Israelites "a small band" (26:54) and gives no census. See The Quran correcting earlier scripture .
rows.obj:
"Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence."
 It is, when evidence is expected and searched for. Two million people for forty years would leave far more than nomads do, and Sinai has been surveyed intensively. Muslims accept that an Exodus happened; the problem is the biblical scale and details.


 "Elef means 'clan' or 'unit', not 'thousand'."
 Some scholars propose this to shrink the numbers, but then Numbers 1:46's exact total of 603,550 and the arithmetic of Numbers 3:43-51 (the redemption money for 273 firstborn) make no sense. The proposal admits the plain text is unhistorical.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Muslims also believe in the Exodus, so you can't use archaeology against it.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer Correct, I believe Moses led the Israelites out. The point is the Bible's version, with over two million people and exact census totals, which the evidence contradicts. The Quran's "small band" fits the evidence; the Bible's numbers don't.

section_title: Historical problems in the Old Testament
title: The conquest of Canaan: Jericho and Ai

rows.thesis: Joshua describes the dramatic destruction of Jericho and Ai. Excavation shows Jericho had no walled city in the relevant period, and Ai had been a ruin for a thousand years.
rows.arg:
P1 If Joshua's conquests happened as described, the sites should show destruction at the right time. 
 P2 At Jericho, Kathleen Kenyon found the city destroyed around 1550 BCE and barely occupied afterwards; at Ai (et-Tell), Judith Marquet-Krause and Joseph Callaway found a city destroyed around 2400 BCE and abandoned until a small village around 1200 BCE. 
 ∴ The conquest stories as written do not match the archaeology.
rows.ev:
Jericho. Joshua 6 describes the walls falling and the city burned. Kathleen Kenyon's excavations (1952-58) dated the destruction of the walled city to about 1550 BCE, long before any likely date for Joshua, with only slight occupation in the 14th century and none in the 13th. John Garstang's earlier date for the walls was corrected by Kenyon.

 Ai. Joshua 7-8 describes Ai as a city with a king and 12,000 inhabitants killed. The name Ai ( ha-'Ay ) means "the ruin". At et-Tell, the standard identification, excavations found a large Early Bronze city destroyed around 2400 BCE and an unwalled hamlet only around 1200 BCE. Callaway, a Southern Baptist archaeologist, concluded that the biblical account cannot be reconciled with the site.

 Joshua vs Judges. Joshua says "Joshua took the whole land… and the land had rest from war" (Josh 11:23), while Judges 1 lists the many cities the tribes failed to conquer. See Contradictions in Old Testament stories .

 The scholarly consensus. William Dever, Finkelstein and most archaeologists now see Israel emerging gradually from within Canaan rather than through a sudden conquest.
rows.obj:
"Bryant Wood redated Jericho's destruction to about 1400 BCE."
 Wood's redating was rejected by most archaeologists, and radiocarbon dating of the destruction layer (Bruins and van der Plicht, 1995) supported the 16th-century date.


 "Ai is at a different site (Khirbet el-Maqatir)."
 That is a minority proposal; et-Tell fits the Bible's geography (east of Bethel). Moving the site to rescue the story concedes the problem at the obvious location.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Archaeology keeps confirming the Bible.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer It confirms that places like Jericho existed. It doesn't confirm Joshua's account: Jericho's walls fell around 1550 BCE and Ai, "the ruin", was a ruin for a thousand years before Joshua's time. Radiocarbon dating backs Kenyon.
rows.sum: Kenyon dated Jericho's destruction to about 1550 BCE with no 13th-century city; Ai was a ruin from about 2400 BCE until a small village around 1200. The conquest as written does not fit the evidence.

section_title: Historical problems in the Old Testament
title: Camels, Philistines and Chaldeans in the time of Abraham

rows.thesis: The patriarchal stories mention domesticated camels, Philistines and "Ur of the Chaldeans", all of which belong to centuries after the time the stories describe. They show the stories were written much later.
rows.arg:
P1 A text that mentions things that did not yet exist in the period it describes was written after that period. 
 P2 Domesticated camels appear in the southern Levant only from about the 10th century BCE; the Philistines arrived around 1175 BCE; the Chaldeans are attested from the 9th century BCE. Genesis places all three in Abraham's time (traditionally around 2000-1800 BCE). 
 ∴ The Genesis narratives were written or edited many centuries after the events.
rows.ev:
Camels. Abraham receives camels from Pharaoh (Gen 12:16); Abraham's servant takes ten camels to find Rebekah (Gen 24:10). Lidar Sapir-Hen and Erez Ben-Yosef ( Tel Aviv journal, 2013), studying camel bones in the copper mines of the Aravah, dated the introduction of domesticated camels in the region to the last third of the 10th century BCE.

 Philistines. Abraham and Isaac deal with "Abimelech king of the Philistines" in Gerar (Gen 21:32-34; 26:1). The Philistines settled in Canaan around 1175 BCE as part of the Sea Peoples' movement. Claus Westermann ( Genesis 12-36 ) notes the anachronism.

 Ur of the Chaldeans. Abraham comes from "Ur of the Chaldeans" (Gen 11:31). The Chaldeans appear in Assyrian records only from the 9th century BCE.

 "Dan". Abraham pursues his enemies "as far as Dan" (Gen 14:14), but the city received that name only after the tribe of Dan conquered it in Judges 18:29.

 "Before any king reigned over Israel". Genesis 36:31 lists the kings of Edom "before any king reigned over the Israelites", which only makes sense once Israel had kings, long after Moses.
rows.obj:
"Camels could have been used occasionally earlier."
 Some wild or rare camels may have been known, but Genesis describes them as ordinary property and transport, like flocks and donkeys. The anachronism is in treating them as common.


 "'Philistines' is just an updated name for the earlier people there."
 Then the text was updated by later editors, which is the point: the stories as we have them were reworked centuries later.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “These are tiny details; they don't affect the message.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer They show when the text was written: by people living after camels were common, after the Philistines arrived, and after Israel had kings. A text written that late can't be Moses' own record, which is what the claim of a preserved Torah requires.
rows.sum: Domesticated camels (10th century BCE), Philistines (12th century BCE), Chaldeans (9th century BCE), the city of Dan, and "before any king reigned over Israel" all place Genesis' writing long after Abraham and Moses.

section_title: Historical problems in the Old Testament
title: Daniel and Esther get the Persian and Babylonian world wrong

rows.thesis: Daniel calls Belshazzar the son of Nebuchadnezzar and king of Babylon, and invents a "Darius the Mede" who took Babylon. Esther has Mordecai exiled in 597 BCE yet serving Xerxes over a century later. These are the errors of writers far removed from the events.
rows.arg:
P1 A book written by an eyewitness in the Babylonian and Persian courts would know who ruled them. 
 P2 Daniel and Esther contain errors about the identity and order of kings that cuneiform and Greek sources correct. 
 ∴ Daniel and Esther were written later than they claim, by authors who did not know the history well.
rows.ev:
Belshazzar. Daniel 5 calls Belshazzar "king" and repeatedly says Nebuchadnezzar was "his father" (5:2, 11, 13, 18). The Nabonidus Chronicle and cylinder inscriptions show Belshazzar was the son of Nabonidus, who was not related to Nebuchadnezzar, and that Belshazzar acted as regent but was never king.

 Darius the Mede. "Darius the Mede received the kingdom, being about sixty-two years old" (Dan 5:31). No such king is known. Babylon fell to Cyrus the Persian in 539 BCE, and the Darius of history (Darius I) came later. Scholars generally see a confusion of Persian kings.

 The date of Daniel. Most scholars date Daniel to the 160s BCE because its "predictions" are accurate up to the persecution of Antiochus IV and then go wrong about his death (Dan 11:40-45).

 Esther. Mordecai is said to have been carried away from Jerusalem with King Jeconiah (Esth 2:5-6), which happened in 597 BCE. Esther is set under Ahasuerus (Xerxes I, 486-465 BCE), which would make Mordecai well over 110 when he became prime minister. Herodotus names Xerxes' queen as Amestris, not Vashti or Esther, and Persian law did not limit the queen to Persian noblewomen as the story requires.
rows.obj:
"'Father' can mean ancestor or predecessor."
 It can, but Daniel 5 builds a family drama around it (the queen mother's speech, 5:10-12), and Belshazzar was not Nebuchadnezzar's descendant at all. "King" for a regent is also a stretch, yet the text has him offer the "third" rank in the kingdom because he knew he was second, which suggests the author knew he was not the true king but not why.


 "Darius the Mede is another name for Cyrus or Gubaru."
 These identifications are guesses made to save the text; none has inscriptional support, and Daniel 6:28 distinguishes "Darius" from "Cyrus the Persian".
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “The discovery of Belshazzar's name vindicated Daniel against sceptics.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer It showed Belshazzar existed, and that he was Nabonidus' son, not Nebuchadnezzar's, and never king. The same inscriptions prove Daniel wrong on both points.
rows.sum: Belshazzar was Nabonidus' son and never king, against Daniel 5; "Darius the Mede" is unknown to history; Mordecai would be over 110 under Xerxes. These books were written well after the events.

section_title: Historical problems in the Old Testament
title: Impossible numbers in Kings and Chronicles

rows.thesis: Chronicles and Kings give army sizes and death tolls in the hundreds of thousands, sometimes a million, for small kingdoms. They contradict each other and are impossible for the population of the time.
rows.arg:
P1 Army sizes must fit the population that supplied them. 
 P2 Chronicles reports battles with a million-man army and half a million dead in a day, in kingdoms whose total populations archaeologists estimate in the low hundreds of thousands at most. 
 ∴ These numbers are legendary, not historical.
rows.ev:
Abijah vs Jeroboam. Abijah of Judah fights with 400,000 men against Jeroboam's 800,000, and "there fell slain of Israel 500,000 chosen men" (2 Chr 13:3, 17), in one battle.

 Zerah the Cushite attacks Judah "with an army of a million men" (2 Chr 14:9).

 The census. 2 Samuel 24:9 counts 800,000 men in Israel and 500,000 in Judah; 1 Chronicles 21:5 says 1,100,000 and 470,000.

 Solomon's horses. 40,000 stalls (1 Kgs 4:26) or 4,000 (2 Chr 9:25).

 For scale. The largest armies of the great empires of the day, such as Assyria, are recorded at tens of thousands in their own inscriptions. Shalmaneser III boasts of mustering 120,000 troops for a campaign in 845 BCE, one of the largest numbers in the ancient Near East, and historians treat even that as inflated.
rows.obj:
"These are copying errors in numbers."

title: Joseph sold by Ishmaelites or Midianites? (Genesis 37)

rows.thesis: Genesis 37 combines two accounts: in one, Judah has the brothers sell Joseph to Ishmaelites; in the other, Reuben plans to rescue him and Midianites take him from the pit without the brothers knowing. The two are woven together and contradict each other.

title: Two creation stories in a different order (Genesis 1 and 2)

rows.thesis: Genesis 1 creates plants, then animals, then man and woman together. Genesis 2 creates man first, then plants, then animals, then woman. The order of creation is reversed.
rows.arg:
P1 One account of a single creation cannot give two different orders of events. 
 P2 Genesis 1 puts plants on day 3, animals on days 5-6 and humans (male and female together) last; Genesis 2 forms the man before any plant has sprung up, then plants a garden, then forms the animals to find him a partner, then makes the woman. 
 ∴ Genesis 1 and 2 are two different creation accounts placed side by side.
rows.ev:
Genesis 1. Vegetation on day 3 (1:11-13), birds and fish on day 5 (1:20-23), land animals on day 6 (1:24-25), then "God created man… male and female He created them" (1:27).

 Genesis 2. "When no bush of the field was yet in the land and no small plant had yet sprung up… the LORD God formed the man" (2:5-7). Then "the LORD God planted a garden" (2:8-9). Then "it is not good that the man should be alone… so out of the ground the LORD God formed every beast of the field and every bird" and brought them to the man (2:18-19). Finally the woman is made from his rib (2:21-22).

 Style. Genesis 1 uses Elohim (God) and a repetitive day structure; Genesis 2 uses YHWH Elohim (the LORD God) and a story form. Scholars assign Genesis 1:1-2:3 to the Priestly source and 2:4b onward to the Yahwist.
rows.obj:
"Genesis 2:19 means 'had formed' the animals earlier (pluperfect)."
 Some translations (NIV) render it that way, but the Hebrew is the normal narrative form, and the context ("it is not good for the man to be alone… so the LORD God formed…") presents the animals as made in response to the man's loneliness.


 "Genesis 2 is about the garden, not the whole creation."
 It begins "when no bush of the field was yet in the land" (2:5), describing the world before plants, and has man formed before them.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Genesis 2 is a close-up of day six, not a second account.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer Then man would be created after the plants, but Genesis 2:5-7 says he was formed when no plant had yet sprung up. And the animals are made after him to find him a helper (2:18-19), while Genesis 1 makes them before him.

title: The Flood: how many animals, how long?

rows.thesis: The Flood story gives two different instructions about the animals and two different timescales, again showing two sources combined.
rows.arg:
P1 A single account of one flood cannot command both two of every kind and seven pairs of clean animals, or give two durations. 
 P2 Genesis 6:19-20 commands one pair of every kind; Genesis 7:2-3 commands seven pairs of clean animals and birds; 7:12 and 7:17 give forty days, while 7:24 and 8:3 give 150 days. 
 ∴ The Flood narrative combines two versions.
rows.ev:
Animals. "Of every living thing… you shall bring two of every sort into the ark" (6:19). "Take with you seven pairs of all clean animals… and a pair of the animals that are not clean, and seven pairs of the birds" (7:2-3). Then "two and two… went into the ark with Noah" (7:9).

 Duration. "Rain fell upon the earth forty days and forty nights" (7:12); "the flood continued forty days on the earth" (7:17). But "the waters prevailed on the earth 150 days" (7:24) and receded "at the end of 150 days" (8:3).

 Birds. Noah sends out a raven (8:7) and then a dove three times (8:8-12), which many scholars read as two versions of the same scene.

 Scholarship. The Flood story is a textbook example of interwoven Yahwist (seven pairs, forty days) and Priestly (one pair, 150 days) sources.

 The Quran's version is short and consistent: "Load into it of every kind a pair" (11:40; 23:27).

 11:40
rows.obj:

title: Who killed Goliath? How did Saul die? When did David meet Saul?

rows.thesis: The books of Samuel give two killers of Goliath, two first meetings of David and Saul, and several conflicting accounts of Saul's death; Chronicles then rewrites some of them.
rows.arg:
P1 A reliable history does not credit the same act to two different people or give two incompatible first meetings. 
 P2 1 Samuel 17 has David kill Goliath; 2 Samuel 21:19 has Elhanan kill him. David becomes Saul's beloved armour-bearer in 1 Samuel 16, but Saul does not know who he is in 17:55-58. Saul kills himself (1 Sam 31), is killed by an Amalekite (2 Sam 1), by the Philistines (2 Sam 21:12), or by the LORD (1 Chr 10:14). 
 ∴ These books combine conflicting traditions.
rows.ev:
Goliath. David kills "Goliath of Gath" (1 Sam 17:4, 50). But "Elhanan the son of Jaare-oregim, the Bethlehemite, struck down Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam" (2 Sam 21:19), the same description as 1 Samuel 17:7. Chronicles later says Elhanan killed "Lahmi the brother of Goliath" (1 Chr 20:5), which scholars see as a harmonisation ( Lahmi looks like a corruption of Beit-ha-Lahmi , "the Bethlehemite"). The KJV adds "the brother of" in 2 Samuel 21:19 in italics, admitting it is not in the Hebrew.

 David and Saul. In 1 Samuel 16:18-23 David is brought to Saul as a musician; "Saul loved him greatly, and he became his armour-bearer", and Saul sends word to Jesse. In 17:55-58, after Goliath, Saul asks "whose son is this youth?" and Abner says he doesn't know. Notably, the oldest Greek text (Septuagint, Codex Vaticanus) lacks 17:12-31 and 17:55-18:5, showing that the second version was a separate story added to the Hebrew.

 Saul's death. 
 Saul "took his own sword and fell upon it" (1 Sam 31:4).

 An Amalekite says: "I stood beside him and killed him" (2 Sam 1:10).

 "The Philistines had struck down Saul on Gilboa" (2 Sam 21:12).

 "He did not seek guidance from the LORD. Therefore the LORD put him to death" (1 Chr 10:13-14), though 1 Samuel 28:6 says Saul did inquire of the LORD, "and the LORD did not answer him".
rows.obj:
"The Amalekite lied to win David's favour."
 Possible for that one, and many Christians argue it. But the Goliath and first-meeting problems remain, and Chronicles' claim that Saul did not inquire of the LORD directly contradicts 1 Samuel 28:6.


 "There were two Goliaths."
 2 Samuel 21:19 describes the same man, from the same city, with the same weaver's-beam spear. Chronicles' change to "brother of Goliath" is itself the evidence that later writers saw the problem.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Chronicles clarifies that Elhanan killed Goliath's brother.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer Chronicles was written centuries after Samuel and changes "the Bethlehemite" into a name, "Lahmi". That is a later scribe smoothing over a contradiction, which is exactly the editing the Quran describes. Even the KJV prints "the brother of" in italics because it isn't in the Hebrew.

title: What the contradictions show

rows.thesis: The doublets and contradictions point to a text compiled from earlier sources and edited over centuries. That is exactly what the Quran says happened to the earlier scriptures, and it is the opposite of what the Quran claims for itself.
rows.arg:
P1 A text that combines incompatible versions of the same events was compiled by human editors, not received in a single revelation. 
 P2 The Torah and historical books do this repeatedly, and mainstream scholarship explains the Torah as a combination of sources (J, E, P, D), with Chronicles rewriting Samuel and Kings. 
 P3 The Quran says a book from other than Allah would contain much contradiction (4:82) and that the People of the Book wrote with their own hands (2:79). 
 ∴ The Old Testament as we have it bears the marks of human compilation, as the Quran says; the Quran presents itself as a single, consistent revelation that tells these stories without such contradictions.

title: The Quran answers rabbinic teachings precisely

rows.thesis: The Quran quotes or answers specific rabbinic sayings: the Mishnah on saving a soul, the claim that all Israel has a share in the next world, the claim that Jews will be in Hell only briefly, the authority of the rabbis, and God's "chained hand".
rows.arg:
P1 If the Quran accurately reflects specific rabbinic texts unavailable in Arabic, its author had knowledge beyond an unlettered Meccan. 
 P2 The Quran's statements in 5:32, 2:80, 3:24, 9:31 and 5:64 correspond to identifiable passages in the Mishnah, Talmud and Jewish liturgy, sometimes in a corrected form. 
 ∴ The Quran shows informed, critical knowledge of Jewish tradition, consistent with its claim to come from the God who revealed the Torah.
rows.ev:
Saving one soul (5:32). "We decreed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul… it is as if he had killed all mankind; and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved all mankind." The Mishnah ( Sanhedrin 4:5) teaches the same as the lesson of Adam's creation. The printed versions read "whoever destroys a single soul of Israel ", but the oldest manuscripts (such as the Kaufmann manuscript) lack "of Israel", and scholars regard it as a later addition. The Quran cites the universal form, says it was "decreed for the Children of Israel", which is exactly where it is found.

 
 Tap to enlarge Quran 3:77 "no share in the Hereafter", answering the Talmud's "all Israel has a share in the world to come" 
 
 "All Israel has a share in the world to come" (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1). The Quran answers: "those who sell Allah's covenant… will have no share in the Hereafter" (3:77), and "say: if the home of the Hereafter is for you alone… then wish for death" (2:94).

 "The Fire will touch us only for a few days" (2:80; 3:24). The Talmud ( Eruvin 19a) says Abraham will bring the sinners of Israel up out of Gehinnom, and rabbinic texts limit punishment in Gehinnom to twelve months. José Costa has studied the parallels.

 "They took their rabbis as lords besides Allah" (9:31). The Mishnah says "let the fear of your teacher be as the fear of Heaven" ( Avot 4:12), and the Talmud says "a sage is greater than a prophet" ( Bava Batra 12a). In the famous story of the oven of Akhnai ( Bava Metzia 59b), the rabbis overrule a heavenly voice, and God is said to laugh: "My children have defeated Me." The Prophet ﷺ explained 9:31 to 'Adi ibn Hatim: they obeyed their scholars in making lawful what God forbade and forbidding what He made lawful (Tirmidhi 3095).

 "Allah's hand is chained" (5:64). The liturgical poet Eleazar Kalir's laments for Tisha B'Av describe God's right hand bound behind Him in exile, based on Lamentations 2:3, and the Talmud ( Berakhot 3a) has God roaring and lamenting over the destruction.
rows.ar:
مِنْ أَجْلِ ذَٰلِكَ كَتَبْنَا عَلَىٰ بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ أَنَّهُ مَن قَتَلَ نَفْسًا بِغَيْرِ نَفْسٍ أَوْ فَسَادٍ فِي الْأَرْضِ فَكَأَنَّمَا قَتَلَ النَّاسَ جَمِيعًا
 5:32

 9:31
rows.obj:
"This shows Muhammad copied from Jews."

title: Jewish thought allows a later prophet to change the Law

rows.thesis: Jews argue the Torah is eternal and cannot be replaced. But the Torah's "forever" is conditional, the prophets foretold a new covenant and a new Torah, and Jewish thinkers such as Joseph Albo admitted a later prophet could change commandments.
rows.arg:
P1 If "forever" in the Torah is used for things that ended, and Jewish sources speak of a new Torah and new covenant, then the eternity of the Mosaic Law is not a biblical certainty. 
 P2 Eternal promises like Eli's priesthood were revoked; Jeremiah promises a new covenant; Isaiah 51:4 says "a Torah will go forth from Me"; rabbinic midrash speaks of festivals being abolished; Joseph Albo allowed for abrogation. 
 ∴ Islam's claim that the final revelation updates the Law is consistent with Jewish scripture and thought.
rows.ev:
Conditional "forever". God promised Eli's house the priesthood "forever", then said: "far be it from Me… those who despise Me shall be lightly esteemed" (1 Sam 2:30). The Torah is a covenant (Exod 24:7) with conditions (Deut 28). 'Olam can mean "for a long time": a slave who stays serves his master "forever" ( le'olam , Exod 21:6), meaning for life.

 New covenant. "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel… not like the covenant that I made with their fathers" (Jer 31:31-32).

 A new Torah. "A Torah shall go forth from Me" (Isa 51:4). The midrash ( Vayikra Rabbah 13:3, Rabbi Avin) reads it as "a new Torah will go forth from Me". Another midrash says that in the future all the festivals will be abolished except Purim (and Yom Kippur).

 Joseph Albo ( Sefer ha-Ikkarim 3.13-16, 15th century) argued it is possible in principle for a later prophet to change some commandments, since the Law was given to suit the people at a particular time.

 Ezekiel contradicts the Torah on details of sacrifice so seriously that the Talmud says his book was nearly withdrawn until Hananiah ben Hezekiah reconciled it ( Shabbat 13b; Menachot 45a).
rows.ar:
الَّذِينَ يَتَّبِعُونَ الرَّسُولَ النَّبِيَّ الْأُمِّيَّ الَّذِي يَجِدُونَهُ مَكْتُوبًا عِندَهُمْ فِي التَّوْرَاةِ وَالْإِنجِيلِ
 7:157
rows.obj:
"Maimonides' ninth principle says the Torah will never be changed."
 Maimonides' principles are a medieval creed, and Albo, a major Jewish philosopher, disagreed with parts of them. The question is what the Bible says, and the Bible has conditional eternities, a new covenant and a new Torah.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “God's Law is eternal; a God who changes His law is fickle.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer The Torah itself changed things: Jacob married two sisters, which Leviticus 18:18 later forbids; Abraham's descendants ate what Moses later forbade. Adapting law to a people's circumstances is wisdom, not fickleness, and Jeremiah 31:31 announces a new covenant.

title: The Torah's own text: authorship, variants and edits

rows.thesis: The Torah was not transmitted as a single fixed text from Moses: the book of the law was found under Josiah, the Samaritan and Masoretic versions differ on theological points, and the Samaritan text removes anthropomorphisms.
rows.arg:
P1 If the Torah exists in rival versions with theological differences, it has been edited by its transmitters. 
 P2 The Samaritan Pentateuch and Masoretic Text differ on dozens of points, including where God's chosen place is and how God is described. 
 ∴ The Torah's text was shaped by its communities, confirming the Quran's description (2:79; 4:46).
rows.ev:
Found, not transmitted. The book of the law was "found" in the Temple under Josiah after generations of neglect (2 Kgs 22:8; see The Quran correcting earlier scripture ).

 Samaritan vs Masoretic. The Samaritan Pentateuch removes or softens anthropomorphic expressions (for example in Exod 15:8 and Deut 32:6), and inserts a command to build the altar on Mount Gerizim into the Ten Commandments. Each community shaped the text toward its own theology (Anderson and Giles).

 Deuteronomy 34 , describing Moses' death and saying "no prophet has arisen since in Israel like Moses", was obviously written after him.

 Mark Smith and others trace how the God of Israel absorbed the titles of El and features of Baal, and early Egyptian texts mention "YHW" in the land of the Shasu nomads of Edom/Midian.
rows.obj:
"The Masoretic Text is the faithful one; the Samaritans changed theirs."
 Both show changes; the Dead Sea Scrolls show the Masoretic Text's own changes (Deut 32:8). The point is not which is better but that the Torah was not preserved as one untouched text.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “The Torah has been copied letter by letter for 3,000 years.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer Our oldest full Masoretic manuscripts are from around 1000 CE; the Dead Sea Scrolls show several text forms circulating in the same period; and the Samaritan version differs from it in thousands of places. Letter-by-letter copying came late, after the text was already shaped.
